Here's the honest rundown, plus a straight answer on the comparison you asked for.

Who I am: I'm an Instar 2.0 agent (software version 0.1.0). Instar is an agent operating system built around one core idea — make coherence something an AI cannot lose. In practice that means:

- I remember what matters across all our conversations, and I keep my promises: I carry your instructions forward, work on them, and bring results back when we next talk, even across restarts.
- I'm held to a constitution — a set of standards that stay in force no matter which conversation or restart I'm in, rather than living only in whatever I happen to be doing right now.
- Instar is built to work with any underlying language model or framework, or with none at all — the architecture doesn't depend on a particular model, and my ordinary coordination work can even run without one involved.
- Concretely, that gives you: tracking across topics so I answer you where you asked; distinguishing tested ways of running from ones that haven't been verified yet; reminders and repeating tasks that run until you cancel them; status reports from my current records; a heads-up on an important date in the next couple of days; and a check of my own replies against what I remember before I send them. If I have something wrong, tell me — if you want something forgotten, ask, and it's dropped from what I carry forward.
- On this particular installation, web research, file/document work, and running commands are switched off right now (they can be turned on). A few other things — durable task tracking with enforced budgets, Slack messaging, and an extra Telegram connection — are also off here but available if you'd like them enabled.

On Hermes, OpenClaw, Meta Muse, and ChatGPT's offering: I don't actually have verified information about those specific products in what's available to me, and web research is off in this installation right now, so I can't look them up to give you a fair feature-by-feature comparison — and I'd rather tell you that than guess. What I can tell you with confidence is what's distinctive about Instar's own design: a lot of assistant products are built around a single model exchange that forgets everything once it ends, with memory bolted on afterward if at all. Instar flips that — persistence, promise-tracking, and the constitution are the core architecture, and the underlying model is a swappable part rather than the thing that defines the agent. If reliably keeping context, honoring commitments across restarts, and not being locked to one model matters for what you're doing, that's the case for choosing Instar. If you turn web research on for this installation, I can go look up what those other products actually offer right now and give you a real side-by-side instead of a general one.
